sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Vǫr** (*vor*) ​— The ‌Careful One, ‌Oath-Goddess · ​Goddess of ​Wisdom and Knowledge ​— belongs ​to the ​Norse tradition, ‌where she is ​catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Wisdom, Oaths, ​Knowledge". The ‌name means "The ​careful one, ‌oath-goddess".[^1]

Vǫr ​is one ​of the ​ásynjur, the female ​powers of ​the Norse ‌pantheon, and ​is named in ‌the Prose ​Edda as ‌a goddess ​so wise ‌that nothing can ​be concealed ‌from her. ​Snorri explains ​her name as ‌deriving from ‌a word ‌meaning 'the ​careful one' ​or 'she who ‌is aware', ​and he ​adds that ‌she is ​invoked by those ​who wish ‌to know ​what has ‌been hidden or ​what oaths ​have been ​broken. Her ​domain is ‌therefore knowledge in ‌its judicial ​and moral ‌sense: the ​truth that ​cannot be evaded.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Vǫr** ‌and serves its ​temple at ‌[vǫr.com](https://punicodex.com/vor/). The ​restoration preserves ​the ǫ ​(o with ogonek) ‌that the ​ASCII form ​loses, and ​exactly one historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier 1. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*vor* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Old Norse ​as **Vǫr**. ​Etymologically it ​means "The ​careful one, ​oath-goddess"[^1]. The ‌word ​*vǫr* is ​related to ‌concepts of ​watchfulness, caution, ‌and awareness; ​some scholars ‌connect it ​to the ​verb ​*vara*, 'to ​be aware, ​to warn'. ‌Snorri's etymology ​makes her ‌the goddess ​from whom ‌nothing ​is concealed, ‌an interpretation ​that fits ‌her role ​as a ​knower of ‌oaths and ‌hidden things.[^2]

‌The ​ASCII form ​*vor* survives ‌only because ​the early ​domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration **Vǫr** ​recovers the ‌ǫ (o ‌with ogonek) ​directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The original ‌carries a ‌distinctive vowel ‌letter, and ‌exactly one ​historically valid ‌Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**v** ​→ **V** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**o** → ​**ǫ** — ‌O with ​ogonek: nasalized ‌vowel
- ​**r** ‌→ **r** ‌— Same

​The project ​holds the ​domain **vǫr.com** ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed., s.v. Vǫr.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/vɔr/** ​— ​Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- ‌**V-** ​— Voiced ‌labiodental ​fricative ‌[v]
- ​**-ǫ-** ​— ​The vowel ​[ɔ] ​rendered ‌with ogonek, ​a ‌nasalized ​back rounded ‌vowel
​- ‌**-r** — ​Alveolar ‌trill ​or tap ​[r]

‌For ‌the modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​'VOR' ​— one ‌syllable, ​with ​a rounded ‌'o' ​similar to ‌the ​vowel ​in English ​'or' ​but ‌more open.

‌Kindred ​and ‌historical forms ​of ​the ‌name:

- ‌**Old ‌Norse** ‌— Vǫr, ​the ‌careful, ​all-knowing goddess
​- ​**Modern ‌Icelandic** — ​Vör, ​in ​modernized orthography

‌Vǫr ​is ​Tier 1 ​because ‌the ​Norse form ‌preserves ​the ‌distinctive ǫ ​that ‌ASCII ‌loses. The ​restoration ​keeps ​that vowel ​visible ‌in ‌the domain ​name.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is preserved ‌in ​medieval ​Icelandic manuscripts ​in ​the ​Latin alphabet ‌as ​**Vǫr** ​— Old ‌Norse ​(North ‌Germanic), attested ​13th–14th ‌c. ​CE in ​the ​codices ​of Snorri's ​Edda, ‌recording ​material ‌centuries older.[^1] ​Before ‌the ​Latin bookhand, ‌Old ​Norse ‌names were ​carved ​in ‌the Younger ‌Futhark; ‌no ​runic attestation ​of ‌this ​name survives.

​The ‌scholarly ​rendering proceeds ​step ‌by ​step:

‌- The ​normalized ​Old ​Norse spelling ​uses ‌ǫ ‌(o with ​ogonek) ‌for ​the nasalized ​back ‌rounded ‌vowel.
- ‌In ‌the ​Younger Futhark ‌the ​name ​would have ​been ‌carved ​approximately ​ᚢᚬᛦ, although ​the ‌exact ​runic spelling ​is ​hypothetical.
‌- The ​Unicode ‌form ​**Vǫr** is ‌a ​scholarly ‌normalization that ‌distinguishes ​the ​Norse vowel ​quality ​from ‌the plain ‌ASCII ​form.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Vǫr** ​belongs ‌to the ‌Norse ​tradition ​as the ​goddess ​of ​knowledge, watchfulness, ‌and ​the ​uncovering ‌of hidden ​truths. ‌Her ​domain is ‌the ​mind ​that ​notices what ​others ​overlook ‌and the ​oath ‌that ​cannot be ‌broken ​with ‌impunity.[^1]

​### Wisdom

‌Snorri ​says ​that nothing ‌can ‌be ‌concealed ​from Vǫr, ​making ‌her ​a goddess ​of ‌comprehensive ​knowledge.

### ​Oaths

‌She ​is ‌invoked in ​matters ​of ​broken or ​disputed ‌oaths, ‌because she ​knows ‌the ​truth ​behind words.

‌### ‌Watchfulness

‌Her etymology ‌connects ​her ‌to ​vigilance and ​caution, ​the ‌quality of ​mind ​that ​guards against ‌deceit.

​### ​Hidden ​Things

Those ‌who ​wish ‌to discover ​what ‌has ​been ‌concealed pray ‌to ​Vǫr, ​the one ​from ​whom ‌secrets cannot ‌be ​kept.[^2]

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Vǫr's mythology ​is brief; ‌she is one ‌of the ​many ásynjur ​whom Snorri catalogues ​rather than ​narrates. Yet her ​defining quality ‌— that nothing ​can be ​hidden from her ‌— gives ​her a ‌significant place in ​the moral ‌order of the ​Norse cosmos.[^1]

​### In the ​Prose Edda

​In *Gylfaginning* 35 ​and in ‌the þulur, ​Snorri lists Vǫr ‌among the ​goddesses and explains ‌her name: ​'She is so ‌wise and ​searching that nothing ‌can be ​concealed from ​her'. He adds ‌that wise ‌people call upon ‌her when ​they want to ​know what ‌has been hidden. ​The passage ​is short ‌but loaded: it ​makes Vǫr ​the divine guarantee ‌that secrets ​will surface and ‌that oaths ​will be judged.[^2]

​### The ​Oath-Goddess

Because ​she knows hidden ‌things, Vǫr ‌is naturally associated ​with oaths. ‌In a society ​where verbal ​pledges were binding ‌and where ‌perjury could ‌bring divine punishment, ‌a goddess ​who sees through ‌deception was ​a powerful moral ​figure. She ​is not a ‌war-goddess but ​a judicial ​one, the inner ​witness against ‌whom no lie ​can stand.[^3]

​### Modern Reception

​Modern readers ‌have found in ​Vǫr a ‌figure for ​conscience and for ‌the unblinking ​self-knowledge that refuses ‌comforting falsehoods. ‌Her name's association ​with watchfulness ​makes her an ​appealing symbol ​for truth-tellers, ‌investigators, and anyone ‌committed to ​seeing clearly.[^4]
